```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4,
  out.width = "100%"

```

```{r setup}
library(randomPlantedForest)

make_data <- function(n) {
  d <- data.frame(matrix(runif(n * 5, -1, 1), ncol = 5, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("x", 1:5))))
  d$y <- sin(pi * d$x1) + d$x2 + 2 * d$x1 * d$x3 + 3 * d$x2 * d$x3 * d$x4 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
  d
}
```

## Threads

`nthreads` sets the number of threads for fitting, and is the default for `predict()` and `purify()` of the model.
The default is 1.
Threads never change the result: with the same seed, the forest is the same at any number of threads.

```{r threads}
set.seed(1)
train <- make_data(1000)

time_fit <- function(threads) {
  set.seed(2)
  t <- system.time(m <- rpf(y ~ ., data = train, nthreads = threads))[["elapsed"]]
  list(model = m, seconds = t)
}
one <- time_fit(1)
two <- time_fit(2)
c(one_thread = one$seconds, two_threads = two$seconds)
identical(predict(one$model, train), predict(two$model, train))
```

The times are those of the machine that built this page.

## What the time grows with

The default call does three things: it grows the forest until the out-of-bag error stops falling, purifies and prunes it, and coarsens its three-way components.
Its time grows with:

- **the number of rows**, directly and through the number of splits: more data support more splits before the out-of-bag error stops falling;
- **the number of tree families** (`n_families`, 200): linearly, in fitting and in prediction. Fewer families are fine for a first look, and more are usually more accurate;
- **the order** (`max_interaction`, 3): a family can grow into many more trees at a higher order, and purification and pruning work on many more components. No limit (`0`) is often much slower than order 3, and usually not more accurate;
- **the number of predictors**: the possible components number `sum(choose(p, 1:3))` at order 3, 175 for 10 predictors and 1,350 for 20.

The number of splits chosen, and the time, at a few sizes of the data above:

```{r sizes}
sizes <- sapply(c(250, 500, 1000), function(n) {
  set.seed(1)
  d <- make_data(n)
  set.seed(2)
  t <- system.time(m <- rpf(y ~ ., data = d, nthreads = 2))[["elapsed"]]
  c(rows = n, splits = m$fit$splits_oob$n_splits, seconds = round(t, 1))
})
t(sizes)
```

Ways to make a fit faster, at some cost in accuracy or in what the model can show:

- more threads (`nthreads`);
- fewer families (`n_families`), or a lower order (`max_interaction`);
- `split_structure = "leaf_binned"`, which tries split points from quantile bins computed once per predictor;
- `n_splits = <number>` and `prune = FALSE`, which skip the choice and the pruning (the model is then the whole forest).

## Memory

While the number of splits is chosen, families grow one at a time, `nthreads` together, and keep only their out-of-bag predictions and a short record of their splits; the chosen forest is rebuilt from these records.
A family that reaches the estimated stop can wait there with its growing state, so that it can grow on cheaply if the stop comes later; `options(randomPlantedForest.adaptive_pause_gb = 1)` bounds the memory of the waiting families (in GB).
More memory saves time; less is freed and regrown when needed.
The result does not depend on it.

Pruning purifies one family at a time and keeps only the pieces of the components it keeps, so it needs far less memory than `purify()` of the whole forest.
A pruned model stores its kept components, not the forest, whose memory is freed when `rpf()` returns.
`keep_forest = TRUE` keeps the forest (unpurified) in `model$fit`, to prune it again or to use it.

## Saving and restoring models

A pruned model (the default) is plain R data: `saveRDS()` and `readRDS()` keep it as it is.

```{r saverds}
model <- two$model
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(model, tmp)
all.equal(predict(readRDS(tmp), train), predict(model, train))
```

A forest (`prune = FALSE`), or a pruned model fitted with `keep_forest = TRUE`, holds a C++ object, which `saveRDS()` does not preserve:

```{r saverds-trap, error = TRUE}
set.seed(3)
forest <- rpf(y ~ ., data = train, prune = FALSE, n_families = 20, nthreads = 2)
saveRDS(forest, tmp)
broken <- readRDS(tmp)
rpf_is_valid(broken)
predict(broken, head(train))
```

`rpf_marshal()` turns it into a plain R list before saving, and `rpf_unmarshal()` restores it:

```{r marshal}
saveRDS(rpf_marshal(forest), tmp)
restored <- rpf_unmarshal(readRDS(tmp))
all.equal(predict(restored, train), predict(forest, train))
```

`rpf_marshal()` works for pruned models too, with or without their forest, so code that saves models of both kinds can always use it.
A restored model predicts without its training data.
`rpf_marshal(include_data = TRUE)` also stores the training data and the bootstrap samples, which a restored forest needs to be purified or pruned.

The [bundle](https://rstudio.github.io/bundle/) package does the same through its generic interface, which tidymodels uses:

```{r bundle, eval = requireNamespace("bundle", quietly = TRUE)}
b <- bundle::bundle(forest)
saveRDS(b, tmp)
restored <- bundle::unbundle(readRDS(tmp))
all.equal(predict(restored, train), predict(forest, train))
```

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
unlink(tmp)
```

## tidymodels

`rpf()` follows the conventions of tidymodels' [hardhat](https://hardhat.tidymodels.org/): it takes a formula, x and y, or a [recipe](https://recipes.tidymodels.org/), and `predict()` returns a tibble with `.pred` (regression), `.pred_<level>` (probabilities) or `.pred_class` columns, one row per row of `new_data`.

A recipe bundles preprocessing with the model, for example imputing missing values, which `rpf()` itself does not accept:

```{r recipes, message = FALSE, eval = requireNamespace("recipes", quietly = TRUE)}
library(recipes)

# rows with a missing outcome are dropped by hand
peng <- subset(palmerpenguins::penguins, !is.na(body_mass_g))

rec <- recipe(body_mass_g ~ ., data = peng) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors())

set.seed(1)
by_recipe <- rpf(rec, data = peng, nthreads = 2)
predict(by_recipe, head(peng))
```

The recipe's steps are stored with the model and applied in `predict()`.

## mlr3

[mlr3extralearners](https://mlr3extralearners.mlr-org.com/) has the learners `regr.rpf` and `classif.rpf`.
